(Today through Wednesday)...
Issued at 400 AM EDT Thu Aug 6 2026

Today through Friday night...

Synoptic pattern through the next three 12-hour periods will feature 
a rather stagnant set-up between two broad and well-maintained upper 
level features...a trough over central/south-central Canada and a 
subtropical ridge across mainly the southern two-thirds of the 
CONUS, except through the OH/TN Valleys where heights will be more 
neutral courtesy of the southern end of the Canadian trough's axis. 
This will place central Indiana in a sort of saddle point...south of 
any sub-seasonal air, but north of any consistent above normal 
readings.
Quasi-steady flow of small weaknesses curling around this axis, 
casually extending to the southeast of the Canadian trough will keep 
an overall disturbed pattern over the local region, amid 
precipitable water values of 1.70 inches or so per southerly flow 
around a Bermuda high ridging west into the Carolinas.

However, overall weak forcing will keep any scattered to briefly 
numerous showers occasional in nature.  Generally isolated thunder 
will be sub-severe with greatest potential impact ponding of low-
lying areas due to weak storm motion.  Timing of higher chances/ 
coverage of convection will focus around early this morning from 
upper forcing...and then perhaps also mid/late afternoon if clouds 
can partially clear enough to facilitate better daytime heating... 
with both of these periods favored more west of Interstate 69.
The diurnal uptick in clouds/showers Friday will most likely be for 
eastern/southeastern counties ahead of a more southern-tracking mini-
vort coming up the Ohio Valley.  A spatially larger-scale shift east 
of the quasi-stacked trough, across Indiana, could potentially bring 
several hours of scattered rain coverage around Friday night's early 
overnight...ahead of quieter weather to start the weekend.

Higher humidity will be the rule through the end of the workweek, 
with dewpoints nearing 75F Friday on southwest breezes gusting up to 
15 mph.  Cloudier skies to promote smaller diurnal temperature 
ranges from 66-72F in early mornings to a damp 81-86F during 
afternoons.

Saturday Through Sunday...

Synoptically, Saturday morning shows a quasi-stationary surface 
front across northern Indiana, situated along the southern edge of 
an elongated 500mb trough stretching across the Upper Great Lakes. 
Boundary layer moisture transport remains elevated ahead of the 
boundary, with ensemble means from the GEFS and EPS maintaining PWAT 
values near 1.8 to 2.0 inches, representing the 90th percentile for 
early August climatology. HREF probability-matched mean guidance 
indicates convective initiation by mid-to-late Saturday morning as 
low-level thermal advection and weak PVA associated with an embedded 
vorticity maximum traverse the region. Model soundings across 
central Indiana depict MLCAPE values rising to 1500-2500 J/kg during 
peak afternoon heating. Weak kinematic forcing, characterized by 0-
6km bulk shear of 15-20 kts, will preclude well-organized mesoscale 
convective systems, but slow cell motion along the quasi-stationary 
front presents a localized threat for training convection and flash 
flooding. Forecast soundings show a deep CAPE profile with freezing 
levels above 14,000 feet.

By Sunday, the surface boundary will continue to lift to the north 
further into the Great Lakes and have less overall impact on central 
Indiana weather. Aloft an upper-level ridge centered over the 
Central Plains will slowly strengthen with minor height rises across 
the area. 700-500mb temperatures will also warm a degree or two 
helping to build a mid-level cap with will help to suppress 
thunderstorm development. Mesoscale models including the HREF 
members suggest isolated High temperatures both days will range from 
the mid to upper 80s, with heat indices approaching the low to mid 
90s.

Monday Through Wednesday...

The broad synoptic regime during the extended period will feature an 
amplified mid-level ridge across the South-Central Plains and an 
anchored longwave trough over the northeastern CONUS, establishing 
active west-northwesterly flow aloft over the Ohio Valley. 
Deterministic GFS and ECMWF runs, alongside GEFS and EPS cluster 
analyses, remain in general agreement regarding this large-scale 
pattern, though variance exists regarding the exact timing and 
magnitude of embedded shortwave troughs propagating around the 
northern periphery of the ridge. 

There has been a slight trend for the jet stream to be further north 
into the Great Lakes which has led to lower rain chances across the 
Ohio Valley. That being said, the thermodynamic setup will maintain 
strong thermal instability, with diurnal CAPE values frequently
